library(tidyverse)

Exercise 1

Is this an observational study or an experiment? The original research question posed in the paper is whether beauty leads directly to the differences in course evaluations. Given the study design, is it possible to answer this question as it is phrased? If not, rephrase the question.

This is an observational study because we are surveying and gather data without altering any of the subjects involved. That question cannot be answered with this kind of study we can find correlations but not causation. A better question would be “Is there an association between instructor beauty and course evaluations?”

Exercise 4

ggplot(data = evals, aes(x = bty_avg, y = score)) +
  geom_jitter()

What was misleading about the other scatter plot was the clustering. Before it was spaced out and over plotted over the same point. With geom_jitter we get to add some randomness to get clusters of data that more visually striking that perfectly segmented data that overlaps.

Exercise 6

library(ggplot2)

# 1. Residuals vs Fitted (Linearity & Equal Variance)
ggplot(m_bty, aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", color = "darkblue", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Residuals vs Fitted",
       x = "Fitted Values", y = "Residuals") +
  theme_minimal()
## Warning: `fortify(<lm>)` was deprecated in ggplot2 4.0.0.
## ℹ Please use `broom::augment(<lm>)` instead.
## ℹ The deprecated feature was likely used in the ggplot2 package.
##   Please report the issue at <https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/issues>.
## This warning is displayed once per session.
## Call `lifecycle::last_lifecycle_warnings()` to see where this warning was
## generated.
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

# 2. Histogram of Residuals (Normality)
ggplot(m_bty, aes(x = .resid)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Histogram of Residuals",
       x = "Residuals", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

# 3. Normal Q-Q Plot (Normality)
ggplot(m_bty, aes(sample = .resid)) +
  stat_qq(color = "steelblue", alpha = 0.5) +
  stat_qq_line(color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Normal Q-Q Plot of Residuals",
       x = "Theoretical Quantiles", y = "Sample Quantiles") +
  theme_minimal()

# 4. Residuals vs Order (Independence)
ggplot(m_bty, aes(x = 1:nrow(evals), y = .resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Residuals vs Order",
       x = "Order of Data Collection", y = "Residuals") +
  theme_minimal()

  1. Linearity — Residuals vs Fitted The residuals should be randomly scattered around 0 with no patterns.The plot shows roughly random scatter. though with some clustering at higher fitted values which is due the the left skewedness. The condition is kind of satisfied but not perfectly.

  2. Nearly Normal Residuals — Histogram & Q-Q Plot This histogram will show a left-skewed distribution show that score is left-skewed as well.

  3. Constant Variability — Residuals vs Fitted Looking at the spread of residuals across fitted values, there is some evidence of the variance being not constant meaning that residuals appear more compressed at higher n fitted values due to the ceiling effect at 5.0.

  4. Independence — Residuals vs Order The residuals vs order plot shows no time-based pattern or trend.

Exercise 9

the equation of the line that represents color pictures is Score = β0+β1×bty_avg+β^2×(1) which equals to = score = 3.74734 + 0.07416 * bty_avg + 0.17239 Two professors who receive the same beauty rating, the professor with a color photo would have a higher score. Males tend to have higher scores than women.

# Residuals vs Fitted
ggplot(m_full, aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", color = "orange", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Residuals vs Fitted (Final Model)",
       x = "Fitted Values", y = "Residuals") +
  theme_minimal()
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

# Q-Q Plot
ggplot(m_full, aes(sample = .resid)) +
  stat_qq(color = "steelblue", alpha = 0.5) +
  stat_qq_line(color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Q-Q Plot (Final Model)") +
  theme_minimal()

# Histogram of residuals
ggplot(m_full, aes(x = .resid)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Histogram of Residuals (Final Model)",
       x = "Residuals") +
  theme_minimal()

# Residuals vs Order
ggplot(m_full, aes(x = 1:nrow(evals), y = .resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Residuals vs Order (Final Model)",
       x = "Order", y = "Residuals") +
  theme_minimal()

The conditions for this model are not met. This is indicated by the residuals being nearly normal and slightly left-skewed. The variability is also nearly constant.

Exercise 17

Yes, this sampling design does have implications for the independence condition. Since each row represents a course rather than a professor, and professors teach multiple courses, multiple observations come from the same professor. Rows sharing a professor are not truly independent of one another, as a professor’s characteristics (teaching style, personality, appearance) will influence all of their course evaluations similarly. This violates the independence condition and means standard errors may be underestimated.

Exercise 19

No, I would not be comfortable to generalize my conclusions to apply to professors generally at any university. There are so many university in America and we need a sample size large enough to represent that to even get close to any generalizations. Not to mention different communities value different attributes so it may not even prove worthwhile to do a sample that large.
